description.p: Spiral is a GTK4 and libadwaita file manager for Wayland desktops that come without one. It follows the GNOME design and adds a file chooser portal backend, so applications that open and save files through the portal get the same picker.

ul.li: Grid, list and column views, tabs, and a places sidebar with devices, bookmarks and favorites
Copy, move, trash, rename and duplicate with progress, conflict handling and undo
Archive extraction and creation with the tools installed on the system
Sandboxed thumbnails, drag and drop, and "Open in Terminal"
The org.freedesktop.FileManager1 service, so browsers and chat apps can show a file in its folder

description.p: The file chooser makes the folder New Folder asks for, its type filters match the suffixes GTK applications send, and its sidebar leaves the tags out when a file is being saved. A window made wider, a maximized chooser among them, gets as many grid columns as fit. "just setup-portal" also sends the file dialogs of Qt applications to the chooser, from the next login.

The selection follows the files. When selected items are trashed, deleted or moved away, the item that takes their place is selected and has the keyboard, so the arrow keys carry on from there instead of starting at the top; a selected file that is renamed, or changed by another program, stays selected; and "Extract Here" selects what the archive left.

A file carries one tag at a time, and picking another replaces it. A tag lists a folder once, whatever paths it was seen under, and rows washed with a tag's colour show the hover. In the column view a tag is a single column, every column keeps its own folder's order, and a folder of images no longer turns the columns into a grid.
Properties tells hard disks from SSDs and names the kind of drive in a word: NVMe, SSD, HDD or USB drive.

Enter in the search box opens the first result, which stays selected until another is picked, and Down takes the keyboard to the results. Escape or Back ends a search and stays in the folder, with the result selected there, or the folder in it that holds the result. Up selects the folder it came from, Back the folder it came through where nothing else was selected, and the side buttons of a mouse go back and forward.

Ctrl+O opens, Ctrl+Return and Shift+Return open folders in a new tab or a new window, Ctrl+I shows the properties, Ctrl+M makes links, Ctrl+Alt+O opens the folder a search result or a favorite is in, and F10 opens the menu of the current folder. The shortcuts work whether or not the context menu offers the entries they stand for.

Trash lists where each item was trashed from and when, and sorts by that date. A copy, move, extraction or archive that lands in another folder ends with a toast that opens it, with what arrived selected, and operations still running when the last window closes are counted in a notification, which says when they are done or what went wrong. Items taken out of Favorites come back with the Undo on the toast. "New Folder with Selection…" gathers several items into a folder named after what their names share, "Copy Network Address" copies the address of a server, and a name longer than the filesystem takes is refused while it is typed.

Properties is laid out as the preferences are. It tells when a file was created, where a link points and where a trashed item came from, each with a button to the folder, and a folder has a Disk page with how full the disk is and what the volume and the drive are: format, label, mount point, subvolume, compression, encryption, model, kind of drive, partition table. The permissions of everything inside a folder can be changed at once.

Colour tags, off until "Colour Tags" in Preferences turns them on. A tag is a name and a colour; seven come by default, and the ones you make take a colour from the palette or one of your own. A file's tags live in its user.xdg.tags attribute, so they survive renames, moves and copies and are the tags other programs read too; an index under the user data dir says which files carry each tag, since nothing can ask every file on the disk, and it is corrected as listings show what is true. The context menu tags a selection from a row of coloured dots, the tags of a file lead its name in every view, the list and the columns wash the row with the first colour while the grid washes the name, and the sidebar lists the tags, opens what carries one, takes drops to tag files, and renames, recolours and removes them.

"Copy to…", "Move to…" and "Extract To…" ask in a dialog attached to the window instead of a file chooser window of its own: folders and nothing else, "New Folder" in the header for a destination that does not exist yet, and the button takes the folder selected or the one on screen. The dialog folds its sidebar away in a narrow window and has a button to ask it back, as the portal chooser now does at its own width. Ctrl+L types a location in the dialogs as well as in the window, and the portal chooser answers Ctrl+R, F5 and Ctrl+S from anywhere in it. A drop on a folder in the list or the columns goes into the folder under the pointer, which is tinted while the drag is over it, and files dropped on Trash are trashed whether the drag arrived as a move or a copy.

A video preview goes on playing when the arrows step to the next file, and a sound file whose length is only known once the pipeline has read into it gets its timeline and the seeking that comes with it. Ctrl+S no longer picks files out by pattern in a save dialog, where that key belongs to the application the dialog was opened for, and "Empty Trash…" does not ask its question over an empty trash.

Opening in a new tab, a new window or a terminal are items of the menu again rather than a submenu, and the colours of a tag are a row of dots in its menu, since a menu that has had a submenu open is not dismissed by a click outside it. Which of the optional entries a context menu carries is a page of its own in Preferences, which are laid out as pages now that there are enough of them: opening in a new tab or a new window, "Copy to…", "Move to…", "Create Link" and "Delete Permanently" are all off to begin with, and a middle click still opens a folder in a new tab whatever the menu shows.

Servers, wherever gvfs has a backend for one. "Connect to Server…" in the main menu takes an address, names the schemes the system can actually use, and offers the servers connected to before. A share that answers opens in the tab in front and joins the sidebar under Network, above it the machines gvfs can find and beside it a button that disconnects it again. Going to a share that is not connected connects it first, so a bookmark or an address typed into the path bar reaches the server without the dialog being opened at all. Without gvfs there are no network locations, and Spiral says so rather than offer an address it has no way to open, and "Network Locations" in Preferences takes the whole of it away for those who have no server to reach.

Renaming takes a whole selection: F2 on several files opens a dialog that gives them all a shared name with numbers after it, or replaces some text of the old names with other text, listing the names it would give as the rule is typed and refusing to rename while two of them would collide. The lot is one entry in the operations list and one undo. "New Document" offers what is in the templates folder, a document per file and a submenu per folder, and both it and "New Folder…" ask for a name before they make anything, with everything but the extension selected.

A drag held for a moment over a folder, a breadcrumb or a sidebar entry opens it, so files can be carried somewhere that is not on screen when the drag starts, and files dropped on Trash are trashed. Ctrl+S selects the names matching a pattern and Ctrl+Shift+I turns the selection round. Escape stops a folder or a search that is still coming in and keeps what has arrived, Ctrl+0 is normal size, and Alt with a digit goes to that tab from anywhere in the window. Folders open in a new window as well as a new tab, a device met in a folder can be unmounted or ejected from there, and the ways of opening are gathered under one entry so the menu of a file is shorter. A folder opened now takes the keyboard with it, and submenus open beside their item instead of moving the menu out from under the pointer.

The file chooser searches the folder it is showing, and only that one, and sorts from its header; it keeps the view and the order it was left in apart from the file manager's own. Answers that cost the disk — which terminals are installed, what the bookmarks file says, whether gvfs keeps per-folder metadata — are no longer fetched again on every change of the selection, and a picture from a share is decoded where a picture from the disk already was, off the thread drawing the window.

Big folders open in a fraction of the time and scroll without stutter. A folder that does not fit in one batch of its listing is shown once, complete and in order, instead of arriving unsorted and being replaced twice; only the view on screen holds the folder, so the two views not showing no longer bind every row it changes; the grid keeps cells for the columns that fit the window rather than for the twenty it may ever have; and a cell's tooltip is answered when the pointer asks instead of being set on every bind, which cost a style lookup per cell. Opening a folder of three thousand photos takes a fifth of the processor time it took on the thread drawing the window.

Thumbnails are asked for only once their cell is on screen and the folder is in order, and a screenful is made from the top down rather than in the order the cells happened to be bound. A thumbnailer that ran out of time or could not be started leaves no note, so the file is tried again on the next visit; only the notes Spiral left itself are read, not those gnome-desktop leaves; and where several thumbnailers claim a type they are taken by name and tried in turn, so one that lacks a codec hands the file to the next. Pictures larger than a limit in the settings are left with their icon, a thumbnailer stands aside for the window it draws into, and the debug log accounts for every request.

Text in the preview has line numbers, on the colour of the page. A video opens in its own proportions, read from the header of its container when the cache holds no thumbnail, instead of snapping to them once it plays. An application whose desktop entry asks for a terminal is given the one from Preferences, so a terminal editor works as a default.

Bubblewrap is now required. Thumbnailers, the PDF previewer and the archive tools are decoders fed files nobody here wrote, and all three used to run unconfined where bubblewrap was missing, while images with no thumbnailer of their own were decoded inside the window itself. None of that happens any more: without the sandbox they are not run, and Spiral tries it once at startup and says what is wrong with it rather than showing nothing. A thumbnailer or a PDF tool that stops answering is killed after twenty seconds instead of holding a slot for the rest of the session.

Big folders open in about half the processor time they took. A folder is put in order once, when its listing ends, instead of after each batch of files arrives; names are collated once each instead of once per comparison; a thumbnail is looked for when a row is shown instead of for every file in the folder, listed or not; a burst of changes in a folder is answered in one pass; and the selection is read out once a frame rather than on every motion of a rubber band. Item counts under grid icons are remembered, and searching file contents no longer does its reading and matching on the thread drawing the window. The thumbnail cache keeps to a size instead of emptying itself, and generation uses the cores there are.

The sidebar gained Root, the top of the filesystem, and a switch in Preferences for it and for Favorites. The order folders open in can be chosen in Preferences instead of only by sorting one, and a folder that remembers an order of its own still keeps it. Caption lines chosen in the dialog appear at once. The selection is no longer lost when a file in the folder is written, so a pasted screenshot keeps the selection it was given. The star column is as narrow as the star it holds, whatever the word for it in the language of the moment, and an empty star is faded so it reads as empty under any icon theme.

The column view is now optional and starts turned off: with it off the view button and the view menu offer the grid and the list alone. Pasted files, folders and screenshots are selected once they land in the folder. Source code in the preview is coloured, on the window's own background, and text files keep their lines unwrapped. The list drops the columns beside the name as a window narrows, so a name is never squeezed into an ellipsis, and shows the whole of one that had to be cut when the pointer rests on it. Preferences are grouped by what they change, and Tab in the location bar no longer takes the focus away from a half-typed path.

Column view no longer decides the view of every folder after it: a folder that remembers a view of its own gets it back, while columns still survive a move that has nothing else to say. Where the system cannot keep a setting with each folder, that choice now falls to the global default instead of going nowhere at all, and the preference says as much. Opening a window or a tab no longer writes the zoom settings back over themselves, and the program is half the size it was.

A quick preview on the Space key: images, PDFs a page at a time, video, sound and text with source code among it, drawn by Spiral itself in a window that takes the proportions of what it holds before it opens rather than resizing in front of you. The arrows walk the folder without leaving the preview, Page Up and Page Down turn the pages of a PDF, Return hands the file to its application, and Ctrl with the wheel zooms a picture around the pointer, which is then moved by dragging it. Video and sound play through one GStreamer pipeline kept for the whole session, and a sound file shows the cover it carries whether or not a thumbnailer ever saw it. A middle click opens a folder in a new tab, the first arrow key in a folder selects its first item, and a photograph is turned the way the camera held it. Windows, tabs and dialogs let go of everything they held when they close.

A column view, the third way to look at a folder: the path drawn as a strip of lists, one folder per column, with the folder you are in at the right and whatever the selection points at beside it. One click in any other column goes there. Ctrl+1, Ctrl+2 and Ctrl+3 now name a view instead of two keys toggling. Shift and the wheel move the strip sideways, and a drag held near either end pushes it along, so a column off the screen can still be dropped on. A file written after it is created, an image pasted from the clipboard say, gets its thumbnail without a restart.

A click on empty space in a folder takes the keyboard and clears the selection, so Ctrl+A and the other file keys no longer wait for a file to be clicked; the keyboard also comes back after a menu closes and after the navigation buttons. A right click on empty space keeps the selection, and the menu it opens acts on the folder. The search filters button has an icon again.

Two folder panes side by side, off by default and turned on with F3: F6 moves between them, the pane in charge is outlined, and everything outside the view acts on that one. Dropping files asks whether to copy, move or link, which Preferences can turn off. An up button beside back and forward. "Show in folder" from a browser no longer waits twenty-five seconds on a portal deadlock, and opens a window of its own with the file selected.

A new application icon. Files cut to the clipboard are faded until they are pasted, and an image on the clipboard, a screenshot say, pastes into the folder as a PNG. The clipboard keys work with the focus anywhere in the window. Drags start anywhere on a row or grid tile and folders accept a drop across their whole row. Compact, resizable list columns with the type shown as the file extension, and a star toggle that follows the favourites.

Search walks subfolders, filters by type and date and can match file contents. Visible columns and captions dialogs, expandable folders in the list view. Restore from trash, links, Copy to and Move to, Run as a Program, path bar and tab context menus, tabs moved between windows and restored after closing. Password-protected archives. Lock emblems and greyed actions for read-only files, folders that follow outside changes, and the clipboard pastes paths into terminals.

Russian and Ukrainian translations. Sort order remembered per folder. A command line that opens new windows in the running instance on every call: -w, -s, -q. Filesystem calls no longer block the interface on slow mounts.
First release.
